GLOBAL.title: Steam players vs. Twitch viewers
GLOBAL.description: Steam player counts and Twitch viewer counts have a moderate relationship (r = 0.45): the two tend to rise together. Across 6964 matched game/day snapshots, that relationship is a real pattern, not noise (p = 0.0000). The link is loose enough that a game can be big on one platform and modest on the other — treat them as complementary signals, not substitutes.

GLOBAL.title: Top games by potential score
GLOBAL.description: 'Dota 2' is the standout this period. It's clear of the next name on the list, 'Palworld', by a real margin — this wasn't a close call. Potential score is NOT the same metric as the 0-100 Opportunity score used on the Call Sheet: it standardizes Twitch viewer_count and Steam current_players into z-scores (how many standard deviations each snapshot is above/below that period's average across ALL games) and blends them 60/40 in favor of viewers, per game/day snapshot, then averages per game. Because it's z-scores, it's centered on 0 and can go negative (below-average) — it flags titles whose viewership AND player counts are unusually high relative to everything else tracked that period, not just titles with the biggest raw audience.

GLOBAL.title: What drives viewership
GLOBAL.description: A Random Forest model trained to predict viewer count leans hardest on 'current_players', with 'Total_reviews' as its next-strongest signal, for GLOBAL_TOTAL. The model explains most of the variation (R² = 0.90, average prediction error ±1,799 viewers). Take the exact ranking with a grain of salt when R² is low — it means factors outside this dataset (game genre trends, streamer skill, real-world events) are doing a lot of the work too.

GLOBAL.title: Streamer activity by day
GLOBAL.description: Streamer supply isn't flat across the week: Saturday draws the most unique broadcasters during GLOBAL_TOTAL, while Sunday is the quietest, roughly 9% fewer streamers active. More streamers on Saturday means more competition for the same audience, so a big crowd there doesn't automatically mean an easy night — pair this with the viewer-per-streamer chart below to see which days are actually easiest to stand out on.

GLOBAL.title: Viewer engagement by hour
GLOBAL.description: Average viewership across a 24-hour UTC cycle peaks at 02:00 during GLOBAL_TOTAL. That's roughly 2.7× the average viewership of the quietest hour (14:00) — going live near the peak reaches the largest possible pool of viewers, but remember the Signal Board factors in streamer competition too, which can make an off-peak hour the smarter play for standing out.

GLOBAL.title: Peak-hour game market share
GLOBAL.description: At the single busiest hour of the day during GLOBAL_TOTAL, 'Just Chatting' pulls in the largest slice of viewership (22.3% of peak-hour viewers). Everything outside the top 5 is grouped into 'Others', which still adds up to 59.9% of peak-hour viewership — a reminder that the long tail of less-tracked games is collectively a real audience, even if no single one of them cracks the leaderboard. Ranked from the top slice clockwise.

GLOBAL.title: Viewer-per-streamer ratio by day
GLOBAL.description: Sunday gives streamers the best payoff during GLOBAL_TOTAL: the most viewers per streamer, meaning less competition per unit of audience. Thursday is the weakest, about 23% lower. This is the real efficiency signal behind the Opportunity score's saturation component — a day can have huge total viewership (see the activity chart above) and still be a bad day to stream, if the streamer count grew even faster.

GLOBAL.title: Predicting rising games
GLOBAL.description: The real test for any 'trending' metric isn't how big a game looks today — it's whether that signal predicts tomorrow's growth. Comparing three candidate signals against each game's next-day viewer change for GLOBAL_TOTAL, 'Peak Players' comes out ahead (r = -0.006). That suggests a simpler signal ('Peak Players') actually predicts tomorrow's growth better than the built-in Potential score does.

GLOBAL.title: Viewer count distribution
GLOBAL.description: The typical stream during GLOBAL_TOTAL pulls a median of 586 viewers, but the top 10% of snapshots reach 2,400+ — viewership is heavily right-skewed, dominated by a small number of very large streams. About 71% of all snapshots sit under 1,000 viewers. That's why averages elsewhere on this site can look inflated by a handful of giants: medians and percentiles tell the more honest story of what a typical stream actually looks like.
